title: TB8-03175
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Principal Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, his common-law spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the Minor Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Principal Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, his common-law spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the Minor Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection. The Appellants have submitted new evidence in support of this appeal and request an oral hearing before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). The Appellants ask the RAD to find them to be Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellants ask the RAD to refer the matter back to a different member of the RPD for a redetermination. Background

The Appellants allege that they fear persecution by the police and broader community in Nigeria as a result of the Principal Appellant's sexual orientation as a bisexual. The Appellants allege that the Principal Appellant engaged in his most recent homosexual relationship in Nigeria while his common-law spouse and daughter resided in the United States, where the Minor Appellant was born. They allege that on a trip to the USA to visit his spouse and daughter, the Principal Appellant was called by his brother to tell him his homosexual partner was caught in Nigeria, and had named the Principal Appellant to police. The Appellants came to Canada and advanced their refugee claim.

The Appellants' claim for refugee protection was heard on December 4, 2017. By a decision dated December 28, 2017, the RPD rejected the claim. The determinative issue before the RPD was the country of reference for the Minor Appellant, a citizen of the USA with no claim against that country, and credibility for the adult Appellants, as well as a lack of subjective fear.1 The RPD found that the Principal Appellant was not a credible witness and therefore did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he is a bisexual or that he is facing more than a mere possibility of persecution in Nigeria. As his spouse's claim was based entirely on that of the Principal Appellant, her claim also failed for lack of credibility.
On appeal to the RAD, the Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its credibility analysis by incorrectly assessing the evidence and/or by focussing on peripheral or tangential issues.2 DETERMINATION

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD accepts the appeal of the adult Appellants and refers the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. The RAD is unable to confirm or set aside the RPD's decision without hearing evidence with respect to the Principal Appellant's credibility relating to his same-sex relationship(s) and the precipitating event which caused him to flee Nigeria.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I confirm the decision of the RPD in respect of the Minor Appellant on the basis of country of reference, that she is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal in respect of the Minor Appellant is dismissed. ANALYSIS Role of the RAD

For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, the RAD applies the standard of correctness, as per Huruglica.3 In assessing issues involving credibility of oral testimony, the RAD applies the RAD modified standard of reasonableness where the RAD determines the RPD had a meaningful advantage in assessing oral testimony.4 Admissibility of Evidence Submitted on Appeal

I note that the Appellants have submitted two items as new evidence in support of the present appeal: (1) an Invitation to Police from Nigeria, dated XXXX XXXX, 2018; and (2) an internet print-out showing the existence of a club called "XXXX" in Nigeria, dated XXXX XXXX, 2014. As the determinative issue in this appeal is the credibility determination which necessitates that the case be reheard before the RPD, I need not address the Appellants' new evidence submitted on appeal, as they will have the opportunity to submit this evidence to the RPD in accordance with the Rules. For the same reason, the Appellants' request for an oral hearing is denied. Merits of the Appeal The RPD was correct in its finding that the Minor Appellant is not a Convention Refugee or Person in need of protection

The RPD noted in its Decision that the Minor Appellant is a citizen of the United States. The Principal Appellant was asked at the hearing if the Minor Appellant had any claim against the USA or any fear of return there, and he confirmed that she did not. The RPD thus correctly rejected her claim,5 and I agree. No arguments were advanced on behalf of the Minor Appellant on appeal. As such, the appeal of the Minor Appellant is dismissed. The RPD Erred in its credibility analysis with respect to the adult Appellants

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in basing its negative credibility findings almost entirely on a lack of corroborating documents where no inconsistencies or discrepancies in the Appellants' documentary or oral evidence were identified.6 The Appellants cite jurisprudence to support their contention that it is an error for the RPD to reject their evidence solely because it was not corroborated by documents, as this erodes the presumption of truth that their testimony and other documentary evidence ought to be afforded. There is merit in the Appellants' argument.

It is clear that the RPD based its negative credibility determination on a lack of corroborative documentary evidence to support the Principal Appellant's claims that: a. He attended school with XXXX, his first homosexual partner;7 b. XXXX lived in XXXX at the same time as the Principal Appellant;8 c. XXXX lived and worked in XXXX at the same time as the Principal Appellant;9 d. The Principal Appellant's first divorce was a result of his first wife's discovery of his sexual orientation;10 and e. There were no photos of XXXX, the Principal Appellant's first homosexual partner.11 Without citing any inconsistencies or discrepancies in the Appellants' testimony or other documentary evidence, the RPD found that there was no corroborating evidence that XXXX lived in Nigeria, and thus, the RPD was not satisfied that the Principal Appellant was in a bisexual relationship with XXXX, as alleged.

In addition, the RPD disbelieved the Principal Appellant's allegation that he had a second same-sex partner, XXXX, whom he had met at a friend's wedding, because the Principal Appellant was not able to provide documentary evidence such as an invitation to the wedding at which he met XXXX, or photos of the wedding the two men attended. The lack of any documentation to support the existence of XXXX resulted in a negative credibility finding regarding the Principal Appellant's second alleged same-sex partner, absent any stated reason for the RPD to disbelieve the Principal Appellant's testimony with respect to XXXX.12

Lastly, the RPD made a negative credibility finding about the Principal Appellant's third, and most recent same-sex partner, XXXX XXXX, because the Appellants did not provide documentary evidence of the existence of the club in which the Principal Appellant alleges he met XXXX, and because of lack of photo identification for XXXX. The RPD put little weight on the photos which were submitted - alleged to be photos of the Principal Appellant and XXXX together - because there was no date stamp or other information about where, when or with whom the photos were taken, and because the photos were not verified by a notary.13 As a result, the RPD found that without photo identification for XXXX or a "notarized photograph" of him, the Panel was unpersuaded that XXXX lived in Nigeria or had a same-sex relationship with the Principal Appellant as alleged.14

The RPD ultimately concluded that the Principal Appellant did not have any homosexual relationship in Nigeria as alleged.15 It is noteworthy that the RPD did not point to any discrepancies, omissions or inconsistencies in the Appellants' evidence other than the lack of corroborating documentation cited above on which to rebut the presumption of truthfulness which must be afforded to their testimony and to ground its negative credibility finding.

After conducting my own analysis of the record, it is clear that the Appellants' RPD hearing consisted largely of questions requiring simple "yes" or "no" responses from the Principal Appellant, and very few questions about the events which the Appellants allege precipitated their decision not to return to Nigeria and to instead travel to Canada to initiate a refugee claim. I note one inconsistency between the testimony and the Principal Appellant's Narrative, specifically whether the Principal Appellant's same-sex partner, XXXX XXXX, was caught engaging in homosexual acts in a hotel (per testimony) or in the washroom of a club (per his Narrative), but this inconsistency remained completely unexplored by the Panel. Thus, I find that the central elements of the Appellants' claim were insufficiently tested at the first hearing. The RPD's negative credibility findings which were based simply on a lack of corroborating evidence, without more, are insufficient to sustain its determination that the Appellants are not credible. In this respect, the RPD erred. Given my review of the Appellants' hearing which indicates that their evidence was insufficiently tested to allow me to confirm or set aside the RPD's decision, I must allow the appeal and return the claim to the RPD for the Appellants' evidence to be heard by a differently-constituted panel.

In addition, I would also note that the RPD faulted the Appellants for a lack of subjective fear, as demonstrated by the period of time they were in the USA prior to seeking refugee protection in Canada. Specifically, the RPD faulted the Appellants for not providing documentary evidence that they consulted a lawyer in the USA to investigate the possibility of seeking asylum there,16 which again I find to be a negative finding based solely on lack of corroborative documents and which therefore cannot stand. The RPD also faulted the Appellants for their illegal entry into Canada as indicative of a lack of subjective fear of persecution in Nigeria.17 It is trite to say that illegal entry into Canada for the purposes of seeking asylum is not indicative of a lack of subjective fear of persecution in one's country of origin. Therefore, these findings that the Appellants lack subjective fear likewise cannot be sustained on appeal.

For the reasons stated above, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Minor Appellant is neither a Convention Refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal in respect of the Minor Appellant is dismissed.

After a review of the RPD's reasons, the record, and the Appellants' testimony, there are unresolved questions that need to be answered and evidence which needs to be sufficiently tested before a finding can be made in respect of the adult Appellants' claim. The RAD is unable to confirm or set aside the RPD's decision without hearing evidence with respect to the credibility of the Principal Appellant on his same-sex relationships and the events which caused him to decide not to return to Nigeria, which remained largely untested after the first RPD hearing. Thus, there is insufficient evidence before the RAD to make a finding on whether or not the adult Appellants are Convention refugees or a protected persons and, in accordance with paragraph 111(2)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD cannot substitute a positive decision. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel. In respect of the adult Appellants, this Appeal is therefore allowed. (signed) "L. Gamble" L.
